scenario: Today's embodied AI track asks where a robot policy should get the information it really needs. The headline paper lets a generalist AI model act as an agent that controls the arm directly, beating specially trained VLA policies without any demonstrations. Several studies of vision-language-action (VLA) models question a default choice: whether the action expert should pass gradients back to the vision-language model, whether images must first go through a separate vision encoder, and whether spatial understanding should wait for fine-tuning. On world models, one paper adds depth to handheld demonstrations and another quickly generates shopping-bag manipulation data from a contact model. A humanoid climbing stairs, Atlas on wheels, gravity compensation for a robot arm and a full day of work in a convenience store come from real deployments.

papers.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
papers.authors: Chen Chen, Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, Xueting Li, Jean-Baptiste Regli, Kejia Ren, Petr Švec, David J. Yoon, Matthias Müller, Vladlen Koltun
papers.abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
papers.screening_note: 依据候选原始摘要；未核实信息不加分
papers.summary: Robot manipulation does not have to rely on specialist policies trained on large sets of demonstrations. In this paper a generalist AI model acts as an agent, commands the robot arm directly and adjusts as the task unfolds, with no demonstrations and no task-specific training, and it succeeds far more often than specially trained VLA policies. The authors' reference harness, AMP1, reaches an 85.6% zero-shot success rate on the RoboLab-120 benchmark, against 49.2% for the leading VLA policy, and it succeeds in nearly all real-robot trials across three robots and twelve tasks. The harness supplies no grasping, pushing or placing skills, so the agent works out its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools and calibrating its cameras. A generalist model used directly as the controller may be more general and more robust than a specially trained policy.

papers.title: STEP: Spatiotemporal Training with Explicit Prediction for Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion
papers.authors: Youhao Lyu, Chenghao Sun, Zhenxuan Ding, Shuting Zhang, Ziyang Dong, Wenhao Cui
papers.abstract: For perceptive humanoid locomotion, the relevance of terrain geometry depends on the robot's body state and how both evolve under its actions. Existing work has advanced terrain-aware sensory fusion and cross-modal prediction, improving how visual and proprioceptive information is combined and related. However, feature aggregation alone does not specify which cross-modal relationships should be learned, while prediction between simultaneous observations does not explicitly constrain their action-dependent evolution. We present Spatiotemporal Training with Explicit Prediction (STEP), a one-stage framework that jointly supervises cross-modal relationships and action-dependent state evolution within a shared control representation. Multiple learned queries aggregate depth and proprioceptive tokens into a compact policy state. Bidirectional masked prediction uses each visible modality to predict latent features of the omitted modality, explicitly supervising terrain-body relationships. An action-conditioned predictor maps the current policy state and executed action to the next fused state, with an exponential-moving-average target defined directly in the policy representation space. Simulation comparisons show overall improvements in terrain traversal over evaluated fusion alternatives and ablations, while depth-dropout and delay experiments demonstrate the benefits of both predictive objectives under degraded visual input. Deployed on a 23-DoF Noetix E1 humanoid with onboard sensing, STEP succeeds in 98 of 100 hardware trials across stairs, a 40\,cm platform, a 70\,cm gap, stepping stones, and backward stair traversal without rearward terrain visibility.
papers.screening_note: 依据候选原始摘要；未核实信息不加分
papers.summary: A humanoid climbing stairs or crossing gaps reads the terrain through a depth camera, but which part of the terrain matters depends on the robot's own body state and on how both change after each action. Existing methods either fuse visual and body-sensing features or predict one signal from the other at the same moment, and neither directly constrains how the state changes after an action. STEP adds two prediction tasks during training. It hides one signal and predicts its features from the other, and it predicts the next fused state from the current state and the executed action. On a real robot it succeeds in 98 of 100 trials across stairs, a high platform, a wide gap, stepping stones and walking backward on stairs, where it cannot see the terrain behind it. When camera input drops out or lags, both prediction tasks also keep the policy steadier.

papers.title: Spatial-UMI-Dream: Scaling World Action Models with Metric Geometry for UMI Manipulation
papers.authors: Weiduo Yuan, Ze Yuan, Sihan Liu, Jionghao Wang, Liang Heng, Zhenyu Zhao, Yue Wang
papers.abstract: The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enables scalable demonstration collection independently of a specific robot. However, its moving, close-range gripper cameras entangle camera and object motion without a stable external view, leaving the metric geometry needed for precise manipulation implicit in RGB. We introduce Spatial-UMI-Dream, a 5B spatial World Action Model (WAM) pretrained on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data through two-stage training -- world-only adaptation followed by joint world-action learning -- to jointly predict future RGB, fisheye-aligned metric depth, and actions. Stereo-derived depth makes scene scale and spatial relationships explicit within a unified dual-gripper RGB-D representation. Furthermore, evaluating UMI policies requires testing whether UMI's robot-independent demonstration collection translates into policy generalization across robot embodiments, alongside robustness to environmental changes. We introduce RoboTwin-UMI, a twenty-task simulation benchmark built on RoboTwin with UMI wrist-mounted fisheye observations, enabling controlled, repeatable evaluation of UMI policies under environment and embodiment changes separately and jointly without additional fine-tuning. On RoboTwin-UMI, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieves 79.10% in-domain success and 72.15% under combined embodiment and environment shifts, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline in each setting by 4.65 and 10.30 percentage points, respectively. It also exhibits the smallest success-rate drop under embodiment transfer among the evaluated policies. In a matched pretraining ablation, RGB-only pretraining leads to a 5.75-percentage-point decrease in in-domain success compared with RGB-D pretraining. Across six real-world tasks, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieves 85.0% average success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 24.2 percentage points. Project page: 【14†this https URL†weiduoyuan.com】
papers.screening_note: 依据候选原始摘要；未核实信息不加分
papers.summary: Collecting demonstrations with a handheld gripper, the UMI approach, is cheap and independent of any particular robot, but the gripper camera is close to the objects and moves with the hand. The image cannot tell camera motion from object motion, so the real distances and sizes that precise manipulation needs must be guessed indirectly from RGB. Spatial-UMI-Dream pretrains a world action model on UMI data with depth, jointly predicting future images, metric depth and actions. The authors also build a simulation benchmark that tests changes of robot and environment. When both the robot and the environment change, it reaches 72.15% success, 10.30 percentage points above the strongest baseline, and it averages 85.0% success on six real tasks. Adding depth makes handheld demonstrations transfer more easily to different robots.

papers.title: Should the Action Expert Train the VLM? Action-Token Supervision and Gradient Routing in Mixture-of-Transformer VLAs
papers.authors: Asher James Hancock, Boyi Li, Yuxiao Chen, Shuhan Tan, Wenhao Ding, Thomas Tian, Yan Wang, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.
papers.screening_note: 依据候选原始摘要；未核实信息不加分
papers.summary: Popular VLA training recipes block the gradients from the action expert to the vision-language model, and this paper finds that this default is not always right. Such models pair a pretrained vision-language model with an action expert that outputs continuous actions. Blocking gradients is meant to protect the vision-language model's existing abilities, and the recipes also train it to predict discrete tokens encoding the same actions. The authors vary these two choices separately and find that blocking gradients looks harmless mainly because the action-token supervision fills the gap. In open-loop driving, blocking or not makes little difference when that supervision is present. Without it, letting gradients through cuts trajectory prediction error by about 25%. When both parts are trained together from the start, letting gradients through raises closed-loop driving route progress by about 17%, or about 40% without action-token supervision, and robot manipulation improves as well. Blocking gradients should not be the default recipe.

papers.title: From Pixels to Actions -- Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.authors: Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Penghao Wu, Siyuan Hu, Ziqi Huang, Tianqi Liu, Mingze Sun, Ziyi Wang, Zhongang Cai, Hanming Deng, Quan Wang, Lei Yang, Lewei Lu, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Dahua Lin, Ziwei Liu
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.
papers.screening_note: 依据候选原始摘要；未核实信息不加分
papers.summary: VLA models usually compress an image into features with a vision encoder before reasoning about actions, and this paper finds that this step loses information control needs, so removing the separate encoder gives better and steadier control. Manipulation often depends on exactly the details most easily lost in compression, such as local geometry, edges, depth and subtle state changes. NEO-VLA removes the separate vision encoder. Images pass through light convolutional patch layers and then travel with the language through the whole backbone, so the action expert can draw instruction-aware visual representations from different depths. In controlled comparisons, this native design consistently beats encoder-based versions, and neither full fine-tuning nor scale alone closes the gap. A control policy should not see only the vision encoder's final output.

papers.title: WorldContact: A Contact-Centric World Model for Scalable Robot Learning
papers.authors: Caoliwen Wang, Mengdi Wang, Heng Zhang, Shixun Huang, Siyuan Chen, Chao Liu, Anpei Chen, Zhendong Wang, Peter Yichen Chen, Huamin Wang
papers.abstract: Adapting robots to new objects and tasks requires interaction experience that can be costly to obtain. We present WorldContact, a contact-centric world model for deformable-object manipulation, constructed from a limited set of high-quality trajectories to generate additional training data efficiently. It predicts object dynamics using larger time steps than the source numerical simulator, which requires small integration steps to resolve rapid motion and prevent interpenetration. We evaluate WorldContact across 16 shopping-bag manipulation tasks. State-rollout measurements on a single H100 GPU show a $10\times$ speedup over the source simulator, excluding rendering and disk I/O. We use the generated data to fine-tune an existing vision-language-action policy and deploy it directly on a real robot. In bag lifting, the same policy achieves 65% single-attempt success when fine-tuned on source simulation data alone, compared with 95% when fine-tuned on the dataset expanded with WorldContact. These results support efficient data generation with WorldContact for robot policy adaptation.
papers.screening_note: 依据候选原始摘要；未核实信息不加分
papers.summary: Adapting robots to new objects and tasks takes a lot of interaction data, and physics simulation of deformable objects such as shopping bags is slow because the simulator needs tiny time steps to resolve fast motion and keep objects from passing through each other. WorldContact trains a contact-centric world model from a small set of high-quality trajectories and predicts object motion with larger time steps, rolling out states 10 times faster than the source simulator, excluding rendering and disk time. After an existing VLA policy is fine-tuned on data expanded with it and deployed directly on a real robot, single-attempt success at lifting a bag rises from 65% with simulation data alone to 95%. For deformable-object manipulation, a learned world model can be a cheap source of data.

papers.title: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
papers.authors: Fuhao Li, Wenxuan Song, Qizhou Huang, Ziyang Zhou, Jingbo Wang, Junwu E, Pengwei Wang, Yan Wang, Shunbo Zhou, Haoang Li
papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.
papers.screening_note: 依据候选原始摘要；未核实信息不加分
papers.summary: VLA models mostly inherit their visual representations from 2D vision-language pretraining, and spatial understanding is usually added only during task-specific fine-tuning, so it must be redone for each task. SLA moves spatial learning into continual pretraining. Starting from a pretrained π0.5 policy, it learns to predict actions while aligning intermediate visual features with spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. The authors also unify robot data from many sources, and during training they randomly drop the robot-state input so the model relies more on images. These extra parts are used only in training, and the inference architecture is unchanged. Under eight real-world deployment conditions, it has the highest success rate among the compared methods in every one.

papers.title: Boston Dynamics adds wheels to Atlas humanoid to test whole-body control
papers.abstract:
Boston Dynamics combines classical motor control with whole-body reinforcement learning to power dynamic, wheeled locomotion for Atlas.

The post Boston Dynamics adds wheels to Atlas humanoid to test whole-body control appeared first on The Robot Report.
papers.screening_note: 依据候选原始摘要；未核实信息不加分
papers.summary: Boston Dynamics has put wheels on the feet of its Atlas humanoid as a testbed for whole-body control, and it says plainly that this is not a product. The only new hardware is a custom adapter that mounts an off-the-shelf scooter rim on the existing ankle actuator, and in software each wheel is simply modeled as an ankle that can spin continuously. Classical model-based motor control keeps the robot stable, while a whole-body reinforcement learning policy adjusts pose and force in real time from body sensing and velocity commands to handle unmodeled disturbances and poor contact. All behaviors were learned in simulation and run directly on the real robot, so Atlas can roll fast on flat ground and switch back to stepping over obstacles. The engineer's takeaway is that combining the two kinds of control is more agile than either alone.

papers.title: Make a Robot Arm Feel Weightless with NVIDIA Holoscan 5
papers.abstract: Picture guiding a robot arm by hand while its motors supply just enough torque to support its weight and keep the robot upright. This simple interaction, a...
papers.screening_note: 依据候选原始摘要；未核实信息不加分
papers.summary: When you guide a robot arm by hand and its motors supply just enough torque to hold up its own weight, you can move it with little effort. This is gravity compensation, the starting point for learning from demonstration and working alongside people. It requires computing inverse dynamics from the current joint state continuously and with low jitter. This NVIDIA tutorial builds a three-node control graph in Holoscan that reads joint state at a high rate, computes inverse dynamics with Pinocchio and sends torque commands to the arm. The key is to run the control nodes on one thread to avoid cross-thread handoffs, with queues that keep only the newest sample. Pinning the control thread to one CPU core then cuts the latency of the slowest few runs in ten thousand to about one fifth in the C++ version and by about 9.6 times in the Python version. Jitter in real-time control often comes from runtime scheduling rather than from the algorithm itself.

papers.title: AI WAVE Wrap-Up: AgiBot Reports Results of Its 24-Hour Convenience-Store Livestream, Moving Physical AI Into Real Settings
papers.abstract:
6台精灵G2机器人，连续24小时在岗，累计完成1730项任务……11月3日10:00，智元“机器人打工不能停”便利店直播挑战正式结束，在全网超200万人的围观下，最终4台机器人成功“转正”。
这场直播也是智元AI WAVE的收官之战。从AGIBOT WORLD 2026第四期数据集Physical Agent、G2 Max重载机器人，到Genie Sim仿真平台、Genie Studio 2.0作业平台，再到具身Agent框架Genie Master、GO-3 Preview基座大模型、群体经验学习范式（CEL），七项成果集中呈现了智元贯通数据、模型、本体与场景的全栈AI布局。24小时便利店挑战，则是在真实营业环境中，检验这一体系的实际应用能力。
papers.screening_note: 依据候选原始摘要；未核实信息不加分
papers.summary: Whether robots can keep working in a real store that is open for business is harder to prove than whether they do a single task well. AgiBot kept 6 Genie G2 robots on duty in a convenience store for a full day under a live stream, completing 1,730 tasks in total, and 4 of them passed the assessment and stayed on. The stream closed AgiBot's AI WAVE series of releases, which also included a new dataset release, a simulation platform, an embodied agent framework and a foundation model among seven results. The public account gives only the total number of tasks and the number of robots kept, without success rates by task type, but long, continuous tests in real settings like this are a step embodied AI must pass to move from demos to real jobs.
